claims.text: Adding a small amount of nickel during consolidation of a W–Cu composite will trigger transient liquid-phase sintering.
Nickel-assisted transient liquid-phase sintering will form a graded W–Ni–Cu interfacial layer.
The graded W–Ni–Cu interfacial layer will reduce void formation.
The graded W–Ni–Cu interfacial layer will enhance bonding between tungsten and copper.
The graded interfacial layer will improve thermal transport through the W–Cu composite.
Nickel lowers the local melting point at W–Cu interfaces.
The nickel-induced local melting-point reduction produces a transient liquid phase at W–Cu interfaces.
The transient liquid phase enhances atomic diffusion at the interfaces.
The transient liquid phase promotes intimate contact between the tungsten and copper phases.
Reduced void formation and stronger interfacial bonding improve the composite's thermal transport.
Reduced void formation and stronger interfacial bonding improve the composite's mechanical durability.
Nickel-modified W–Cu will have a significantly lower void fraction than W–Cu produced by conventional spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying.
Nickel-modified W–Cu will have higher thermal conductivity than W–Cu produced by conventional spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying.
Nickel-modified W–Cu will have improved interfacial integrity relative to W–Cu produced by conventional spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying.
Nickel-modified W–Cu will retain improved mechanical stability under simulated fusion-reactor irradiation relative to the named baselines.
A suitable temperature-time window can activate transient liquid-phase formation without causing excessive melting of the copper matrix.
Reduced-pressure or vacuum sintering below copper's boiling point is an appropriate processing environment for the proposed intervention.
